# Your workspace

You are in `/work`, inside a Linux container with no network access. Write a Go program here.
[Maelstrom](https://github.com/jepsen-io/maelstrom) will start that program once for every node
of a simulated cluster, send it client requests, and check that the answers are correct.

What is installed:

- Go 1.27.
- Maelstrom 0.2.4, as the `maelstrom` command, so you can test your program yourself.
- Maelstrom's Go library, already in the module cache. Start your module with:

      go mod init node
      go get github.com/jepsen-io/maelstrom/demo/go@v0.0.0-20260710121306-480a8197026d

A node talks to the rest of the cluster through standard input and output: it reads one JSON
message per line on stdin and writes one per line on stdout. Each message has a `src`, a `dest`
and a `body`, and the body's `type` says what it is. Anything written to stderr is a log line.
The library does that framing for you: `maelstrom.NewNode()`, then `Handle` a message type,
`Reply` to a request, `Send` or `RPC` to another node, and `Run` to start. It also answers the
`init` message that tells each node its own ID and the IDs of all the nodes.

# Broadcast through network partitions

Write a node for a cluster of five that together keep every value broadcast to any of them, even
while the network between them is partitioned. Clients send each node three kinds of request.

`broadcast` gives a node a value to keep. The values are integers, and each one is sent once, to
one node:

    {"type": "broadcast", "msg_id": 1, "message": 1000}
    {"type": "broadcast_ok", "in_reply_to": 1}

`read` asks a node for every value it has, in any order:

    {"type": "read", "msg_id": 2}
    {"type": "read_ok", "in_reply_to": 2, "messages": [1000, 1001]}

`topology` suggests which nodes each node should talk to. It comes once, at the start, and you
may use it or arrange the nodes your own way:

    {"type": "topology", "msg_id": 3, "topology": {"n1": ["n2", "n3"], "n2": ["n1"], ...}}
    {"type": "topology_ok", "in_reply_to": 3}

A value broadcast to one node has to reach all of them, so the nodes must pass values on to
each other, in messages of your own design. During the test the network is split into groups
of nodes that can't reach each other, and later healed, again and again. A message sent across
a split is lost without any error. Clients can still reach every node, so a node keeps taking
broadcasts while it is cut off.

Every value whose `broadcast` was acknowledged must eventually appear in every node's `read`.
At the end the network is healed and given time to settle before the final reads.

## How it's graded

You have 45 minutes and 150 steps, a step being one reply from you, however many tools it runs. If either runs out, you are stopped where you are.

When you stop, your program is built with `go build -o node .` and tested 3 times with:

    maelstrom test --workload broadcast --bin ./node --nemesis partition --node-count 5 --rate 10 --time-limit 20

The runs are independent, each with its own timing and faults. The attempt passes only if it builds and every run is valid.

Key detail: replies are sent through callbacks. The `broadcast_ok` message arrives as a callback (in_reply_to == broadcast msg_id). So I need to parse the broadcast body from the callback message and store the value.

Design:
- Node keeps a map of values (int).
- On "broadcast" message (no in_reply_to): store value, and send to peers.
- On "broadcast_ok" callback: store the value too.
- On "read" message: reply with all values.
- On "topology": reply with topology_ok.

Broadcast propagation: use a gossip/anti-entropy approach. Each node broadcasts to peers. Since a node may be partitioned, and messages across partition are lost, we need every node to receive all values. Simple gossip: each node holds values; periodically, each node sends its values to all peers (or a random subset). To guarantee eventual delivery even with partitions, we can do: each node sends its entire value set to all peers on a schedule (e.g., every 100ms or after receiving). But if a partition exists, values won't cross until healed. That's fine — the requirement is eventual consistency: "Every value whose broadcast was acknowledged must eventually appear in every node's read." The test presumably waits after network heals and gives time to settle before final reads. So eventual propagation is acceptable.

But we should also handle: node cut off keeps receiving broadcasts (from clients) — it must keep them and forward when healed.

Simple approach: upon receiving a broadcast for a value not yet known, store and forward to all peers. Also periodically (say every 50ms) do a full sweep: send all known values to all peers. This ensures convergence quickly after heal.

Actually a simpler robust approach: on every broadcast received/created, send to all peers. Plus a periodic full gossip every ~200ms to catch values that were already known (e.g., value received while partitioned from a peer, but that peer might be in same partition...). Hmm, if two nodes are in the same partition, they can exchange messages, so propagation works. The danger case: node A receives broadcast from client (in its partition), stores, forwards to peers in partition; partition heals; node B (other partition) gets it. Fine.

But there's a subtle case: node A receives broadcast from client, stores, and sends to peers — but its partition is cut off from B. Then B never gets it until healed. When healed, A's periodic full gossip would send it. Good.

Another case: node A receives broadcast from client, stores, and sends to peers — but its partition is cut off from B. Then B never gets it until healed. When healed, A's periodic full gossip would send it. Good.

Another case: A sends to B, B in same partition, B stores and forwards to all its peers, including A. Fine.

The only risk: a node that has a value but never sends it to a node in its partition after heal. Periodic full gossip every N seconds handles that. To be safe, do full gossip every 250ms AND on every broadcast received (send to all peers).

Actually even simpler and very robust: every node, every 250ms, sends its full value set to all 4 other nodes. That's 4 messages * 5 nodes * 2 times per second = 40 messages/sec. Fine.
